messages.label.why: A mode is the name of a set of rules: who can answer, how far your data can go, which limits apply. The name alone decides nothing: the rules do, and the description next to each mode is computed from them. Here you choose which set is active; its rules are changed from «Where your data goes» and «All rules of this mode». Services, language and storage apply to the whole router, whatever mode is active.
messages.label.add: New mode - Starts from a copy of the active one: give it a name, and its description is computed from the rules.
messages.guide.zones.why: The router decides by itself where to send a request, and these answers are its limit. The zones go from nearest to farthest: this computer, your local network, your own server in the European Union, a provider you have a data processing agreement with, any service. I will not ask where each service is: the router works that out from how it is configured and from what you confirmed.
messages.guide.zones.same_host: Only this computer - No request leaves this machine.
messages.guide.zones.lan: Also your local network - For example a server at home or in the office, reachable without going out to the Internet.
messages.guide.zones.private_eu: Also your own server in the European Union - A machine of yours off site, with the region verified and not expired.
messages.guide.zones.third_party_dpa: Also providers with a processing agreement - External services for which you confirmed a data agreement, with an expiry.
messages.guide.zones.third_party: Any service - Including external services without a processing agreement.
messages.guide.grading.why: The detectors find the signals — here is a name, here is a tax code — but where the border between «personal» and «sensitive» falls for a name alone is yours to decide: for a private person it is personal data, for someone handling citizens' data it is already sensitive. A tax code, an identity document, an IBAN, a card, or a name together with an address are always sensitive: those are not a choice.
messages.guide.grading.title: A person's name, alone: personal or sensitive data?
messages.guide.grading.graded: Personal - It follows the answer you gave for internal and personal data.
messages.guide.grading.strict: Sensitive - Any personal datum follows the answer you gave for sensitive data. It is the choice for those who handle citizens' data on behalf of a public body.
messages.guide.confirm.why: When sensitive data could go to an external provider, the router can stop and ask you, one request at a time. The question appears only in the terminal: an application using the API cannot answer, and for it the request is refused.
messages.guide.confirm.title: Do you want to be asked before sensitive data is sent out?
messages.guide.confirm.no: No - What you just chose stands: if a service is allowed, the router uses it without asking.
messages.guide.confirm.yes: Yes - For sensitive data the router asks every time, and without a yes nothing is sent.
messages.guide.attach.why: A file you attach to a request is content like the rest, but it is often larger and less predictable than what you type. So unless you say otherwise it stays inside the perimeter: this computer, your local network and your own server in the European Union.
messages.guide.attach.title: May attachments leave the perimeter?
messages.guide.attach.no: No - A request with attachments stays inside the perimeter.
messages.guide.attach.yes: Yes - They may go as far as the other data, and every exit is recorded.
messages.guide.weak.why: It can happen that the capable models are outside the perimeter and those inside are not enough for a difficult request. The router never sends out on its own: it either answers with what it has, telling you, or refuses.
messages.guide.weak.title: If only a model that is too weak is inside the perimeter?
messages.guide.weak.declare: Answer and say so - The best inside model answers, and the answer says it is below the threshold.
messages.guide.weak.deny: Refuse - No answer, and the reason with the parameter to change.
messages.guide.weak.apiWhy: This profile serves the applications that use the API, where there is nobody to ask. If the capable models are outside the perimeter, the router answers with what it has inside, declaring it in the response, or refuses with the reason.
messages.guide.weak.apiTitle: What does the API do when data would have to leave?
messages.guide.weak.apiDeclare: Answer with what is inside, saying so - The response carries a field that declares it.
messages.guide.weak.apiDeny: Refuse with the reason - The application gets the refusal code, not a weaker answer.

messages.guide.zones.public: How far may public data go?
messages.guide.zones.personalWhy: Internal data are the work material not meant for the public: the name of one of your projects, a company, an internal document. Personal data are about a person: a name, an email address, a phone number. Here you can keep them closer than public data; you cannot send them further.
messages.guide.zones.sensitiveWhy: Sensitive data identify a person — tax code, identity document, IBAN, card — or touch the special categories: health, religion, political opinions, sex life, trade union, origin, genetic or biometric data. Here you can keep them closer than personal data; you cannot send them further. Credentials and texts the scan cannot classify never leave the local network: that is not a choice.

messages.guide.order.why {0} {1}: The router picks the smallest model that is enough for the request: to do that it needs to know which one you consider more capable. I am not asking for scores — nobody can give those — but for an order. Choice {0} of {1}.
messages.guide.order.title {0}: Which of these is the most capable? (place {0})
messages.guide.order.done: Order saved. It is the only measure of quality the router uses: with the request analyzer on it decides who is enough for each question (the first that is enough answers, starting from the smallest); without the analyzer it is half of the score, and the first counts most.
messages.guide.analyzer.why: Before choosing the service, the router can have a small model installed here look at the request to estimate its difficulty. It runs on this machine, sees only the beginning of your request and never the context. For now it observes and reports: it decides nothing, and it will only decide after a measurement recorded on this machine. Without an analyzer, non-trivial requests count as difficult. The model chosen here works for the router and does not answer your requests: if you want it to answer too, add it as a chat model in Services and models.
